text: Every ledger needs a calendar, one of its four C's. This lesson covers what an Oracle Fusion accounting calendar actually consists of, and why these choices ripple through every period-end close for the ledger's life.

An accounting calendar breaks a fiscal year into periods. Defining one means specifying the period type, how many periods per year, start and end dates, period names, and the fiscal year's start month, which isn't always January.

Most implementations use one of two patterns: monthly, Gregorian calendars with twelve periods matching calendar months, or thirteen-period calendars with equal-length periods, often on a 4-4-5 week pattern common with retailers and manufacturers.
Each period needs a clear, unambiguous name, like Jan-25, because users see that name on every transaction and report for years. Consistency matters more than cleverness.
Once a calendar has live transactions posted, changing its structure is disruptive at best, sometimes effectively impossible. Next up, lesson sixteen: period types and adjusting periods.
